text: I’ll represent the leak path as a 0.2 mm-thick helical ribbon following one 30° trapezoidal thread flank. The ribbon runs six turns over the stated 12 mm threaded height; its radial span is the stated 1 mm thread depth. The neck and lid bound its two broad helical faces, and the two cut ends become the inner and outer patches. I’ll first verify the available sweep/helix API before constructing the coarse solid.

The API supports a direct solid sweep. I’ll now make a very coarse CAD ribbon in metres, sweep a rectangular section whose 1 mm direction lies along the 15° thread flank and whose 0.2 mm direction is normal to it, then measure its bounds/volume and render it. This preview is deliberately CAD-only; meshing comes after the shape and face identities are confirmed.

The preview shows the intended single continuous six-turn path and no overlap between turns. The swept solid has exactly six faces: two end caps and four ruled helical faces. I’ll classify those by their generated role (cap area versus sweep-face area, then flank width), not by bounding-box position, and inspect each face’s area and center before assigning the two narrow edge strips to the adjacent neck/lid groups.

The measured cap area (0.2071 mm²) agrees with the 1 mm flank span at 15° times the 0.2 mm clearance. The broad helical faces are 761.04 mm² each, matching the expected 761.17 mm². I’ll now export the four requested patches in one conformal tessellation: each named flank includes its broad contact face plus the adjacent narrow crest/root edge strip, while each helix end is its own cap.
The face classification succeeded, but the exporter’s installed signature does not use a `directory` keyword. I’ll inspect its exact local signature and then call it with the supported path argument.
I’ll re-emit the export step self-contained so the reproducible script imports the exporter and recreates the face classification rather than relying on the failed cell.

The conformal export is watertight (0 open, flipped, or non-manifold edges). I’ll mesh the exact STEP solid with Gmsh tetrahedra, using the STL files as the required per-patch surface exports and matching Gmsh’s six CAD surfaces by their measured geometric roles. Before generating, I’ll inspect the imported surface areas to confirm the correspondence survived STEP translation.

STEP translation preserved all six areas and the 152.19 mm³ volume. I’ll now generate a coarse tetrahedral mesh with a 0.20 mm target size (the 0.2 mm gap edge itself forces at least one layer), retain the four physical patch names, write MSH2, and convert it to OpenFOAM. If quality is poor or the gap is under-resolved, I’ll refine after checking this coarse version.

The coarse Gmsh mesh contains about 139k tetrahedra; conversion stopped only because an empty case lacks `system/controlDict`. I’ll add the minimal mesh-only control file, rerun conversion, and execute the binding bare `checkMesh`.

Conversion succeeded and preserved all four patch names. `checkMesh` in this OpenFOAM build also expects the two standard numerical dictionaries even for a mesh-only case, so I’ll add empty valid dictionaries and rerun it; I’ll also print the boundary file summary to ensure `defaultFaces` is empty.
The boundary file has exactly the four requested patches and no `defaultFaces`; their face counts are nonzero. I’ll provide the minimal required scheme subdictionaries and rerun the binding check.

Topology, patching, volume, non-orthogonality, and skewness all pass, but 38 sliver tetrahedra trigger the one failed mesh check (maximum aspect ratio 6733). I won’t waive a binding defect. I’ll regenerate the same geometry with Gmsh’s HXT 3D algorithm and Netgen optimization, keeping the coarse 0.20 mm surface target, to eliminate those slivers.
The optimized mesh has 184,287 tetrahedra after Netgen removed all illegal elements. I’ll reconvert it and rerun bare `checkMesh`, replacing the earlier polyMesh.

The optimized OpenFOAM mesh now passes bare `checkMesh`: 184,287 cells, one region, maximum aspect ratio 6.36, maximum non-orthogonality 60.75°, and maximum skewness 0.603. I’ll take one final mesh rendering to visually confirm that the converted mesh still follows the complete six-turn ribbon.

The final rendering confirms one continuous six-turn helical mesh with both ends open only through their named cap patches.

Measured/built:
- Neck OD: 40 mm; thread radii 19–20 mm.
- Pitch: 2 mm; threaded rise: 12 mm; single start gives exactly 6 turns.
- Air-gap thickness: 0.2 mm.
- Flank radial depth: 1.0 mm; assumed standard trapezoidal included angle: 30°.
- Helix length: 735.23 mm; fluid volume: 152.19 mm³.
- Mesh: 184,287 tetrahedra, one connected region, four named patches.
- Bare `checkMesh`: **Mesh OK**.

Outputs include `neck_flank.stl`, `lid_flank.stl`, `inner_end.stl`, and `outer_end.stl` under `constant/triSurface`, plus the OpenFOAM mesh under `constant/polyMesh`.

Assumption: because no trapezoidal flank angle was specified, I used the standard 30° included angle. The narrow crest/root edge strips were grouped with their adjacent neck/lid flank patches so the boundary contains exactly the four requested names. No requested property remains unchecked.

The coverage advisory reports complete one-to-one coverage—every one of the 6,528 STL triangles belongs to exactly one of the four requested patches—so this warning is expected and correct for this explicitly grouped four-patch boundary.
